result:
Okay, I'm going to talk about Unfinished Things.

Not big, dramatic unfinished things like novels or symphonies. I mean the small ones.

The sweater you started knitting three winters ago that's still just one sleeve and a lot of good intentions in a tote bag.

The language learning app you were SO committed to for 11 days straight. You can still say "the apple is red" in Portuguese.

The saved drafts. The tabs you keep open "to read later." The half-written text you never sent because you couldn't find the right ending.

We treat unfinished things like failures. Like clutter. Evidence that we lack discipline.

But I think unfinished things are actually proof that we are alive and changing.

You started that sweater when you loved chunky oversized knits. Now you're into minimalism. You started learning Portuguese because you were going to visit Lisbon with someone you don't talk to anymore. You saved 47 articles about sourdough because for a month in 2020, sourdough felt like the only thing you could control.

You didn't finish those things because *you* didn't stay the same. The person who wanted to finish them doesn't quite exist anymore. And that's not failure. That's growth, just with a messy paper trail.

A finished thing is frozen. It's done. It has a period at the end. An unfinished thing is still warm. It still has potential. It's a Schrödinger's project - simultaneously a masterpiece and a disaster until you look at it again.

There's a Japanese concept called "wabi-sabi" - finding beauty in the imperfect and incomplete. We love ruins. We love demo tapes where you can hear the singer laugh. We love sketchbooks more than final paintings sometimes, because you can see the thinking.

Maybe we should love our own incompleteness the same way.

I like to think of every person as a house with a lot of rooms under renovation. One room is perfect, one is just studs and wiring, one you painted a bold color and immediately regretted. But it's all yours. No one lives in a fully finished house. If they say they do, they're lying, or they're not building anything new.

So if you have a drawer full of half-finished things, don't be embarrassed. That's not your graveyard of ambition. That's your compost pile. All that old yarn and rusty Portuguese and abandoned ideas will break down and feed whatever you make next, even if the next thing looks completely different.

What are you leaving unfinished right now without guilt?

I have a few myself. Want to trade?
